blocks.text: Synthetic data generation is the practice of creating training examples using a model rather than collecting them entirely from real world sources, seed examples, templates, or an existing model prompted to produce new task demonstrations.

It has become a practical way to scale up a fine-tuning dataset quickly, especially when real examples are scarce, expensive to collect, or too sensitive to use directly, though it comes with its own set of quality risks covered later in this topic.
1. What Synthetic Data Generation Means

blocks.alt: Seed examples pass through a generator model to produce synthetic examples

blocks.text: Rather than relying purely on collected or hand written data, synthetic data generation uses a model, prompted with instructions or a small set of seed examples, to produce new training examples automatically, which can then be filtered, reviewed, and added to a fine-tuning dataset.
This is not a replacement for real data collection so much as a way to expand and diversify a dataset faster than manual collection alone could achieve.
2. Why Teams Turn to Synthetic Data

blocks.alt: Slow manual collection is compared against fast synthetic generation

blocks.text: Manual data collection and annotation, covered in earlier topics of this module, is often the slowest part of a fine-tuning project. Synthetic generation can produce hundreds or thousands of candidate examples in the time it would take to manually write or annotate a small fraction of that volume.
It is particularly useful for covering rare edge cases that occur too infrequently in real data to gather enough natural examples of them.
3. Using a Larger Model to Generate Training Examples for a Smaller One

blocks.alt: A larger teacher model generates examples that train a smaller student model

blocks.text: A common pattern, often called distillation, uses a large, highly capable model to generate high quality example responses, which then become the training data for fine-tuning a smaller, cheaper model to imitate that behavior.
This lets a team benefit from a large model quality without paying that model inference cost on every production request, since the smaller fine-tuned model handles requests directly once trained.
4. Templated Generation for Structured Variety

blocks.alt: A template with variables produces many filled variations

blocks.text: For tasks with a predictable structure, filling in a template with different variable values, names, dates, product types, is a simple and reliable way to generate a large volume of structurally consistent, varied examples without relying on a generator model at all.

code.content:
# A simple templated generation pattern
templates = [
    "Summarize the return policy for {product_category}",
    "Explain the warranty terms for {product_category}",
]
categories = ["electronics", "furniture", "clothing"]
generated_prompts = [
    t.format(product_category=c) for t in templates for c in categories
]

blocks.text: 5. Self-Instruct Style Generation

blocks.alt: A few seed tasks are expanded by a model into many new task examples

blocks.text: A more flexible approach, often called self-instruct style generation, starts with a small handful of hand written seed examples, then prompts a model to generate many new, varied task examples inspired by those seeds, expanding a small starting set into a much larger one.
This approach trades some of the structural predictability of templated generation for broader, more natural sounding variety, at the cost of needing more careful review of the results.
6. The Risk of Distillation Collapse and Quality Drift

blocks.alt: Repeated synthetic generations can drift in quality over successive rounds

blocks.text: Generating synthetic data from a model, then using that data to train another model, and repeating this process across several rounds, can gradually amplify small errors or biases present in the generator, a phenomenon sometimes called model collapse when it compounds over many generations.

blocks.title: Do not chain synthetic generations indefinitely
blocks.content: Each additional round of generating data from a model trained on previously generated data increases the risk of drifting away from real world quality, so anchoring periodically back to genuine, human sourced data matters.

blocks.text: 7. Mixing Synthetic Data With Real Data

blocks.alt: Real data and synthetic data combine into one mixed dataset

blocks.text: Most practical fine-tuning datasets that use synthetic data do not rely on it exclusively, they blend synthetic examples with a base of real, human sourced data, using synthetic generation to expand coverage and volume while real data anchors overall quality and realism.

blocks.text: 8. Validating Synthetic Examples Before Using Them

Synthetic examples should go through the same cleaning and, ideally, a lighter version of the annotation review process covered elsewhere in this module, since a generator model can produce plausible sounding but subtly incorrect or unrealistic examples that would otherwise slip straight into training.
A useful practice is manually reviewing a random sample of generated examples before scaling up generation to the full planned volume, catching systematic problems early.
9. When Synthetic Data Is Not a Good Fit

Synthetic data is a poor fit when the task depends on subtle, real world nuance a generator model cannot reliably reproduce, or when the domain is specialized enough that the generator itself has weak underlying knowledge of it, in which case the synthetic examples inherit that weakness.
It is also worth avoiding for tasks where factual precision matters most, since a generator model can produce fluent but factually wrong examples that look correct on the surface.
Worked Example

A team wants to fine-tune a small model to answer customer questions about a specific software product, but they only have three hundred real support conversations to work with, not enough for reliable fine-tuning on its own.

They use a larger model to generate an additional two thousand synthetic question and answer pairs, seeded with their real support conversations and product documentation, then manually review a five hundred example sample, catching and removing about fifty examples with factual errors about the product before finalizing the dataset. The combined real plus synthetic dataset produces a noticeably better fine-tuned model than the three hundred real examples alone would have.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying entirely on synthetic data with no real data anchoring overall quality
Skipping validation of generated examples and assuming a generator model output is automatically correct
Chaining many rounds of synthetic generation without periodically returning to real, human sourced data
Using synthetic generation for a specialized domain the generator model itself has weak knowledge of

blocks.text: Practice

Take a small handful of real examples for a task you have in mind, and sketch what a prompt asking a model to generate similar but new examples would look like, including what quality checks you would run on the results before trusting them.
Key Takeaway

Synthetic data generation can expand a fine-tuning dataset quickly and cheaply, through templated generation, self-instruct style expansion, or teacher model distillation, but it works best mixed with and anchored by real data, with generated examples validated carefully rather than trusted blindly.
